To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the risk of death, cardiovascular events and alcohol-related events was significantly elevated in men who were alcohol dependent at the conscription medical examination at age 18 years, and that this elevated risk remained throughout a 35-year follow-up.
In a 35 year cohort follow-up of 50, 000 Swedish conscripts, alcohol intake was associated with increased mortality from all causes, cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality and CVD events.

1) Alcohol consumption is a major cause of death and disability in the Western world, and 2) Alcohol consumption increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and mortality, even among light-to-moderate drinkers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between alcohol use and health, with particular emphasis on the role of alcohol in the aetiology of cancer and cardiovascular disease.
the relationship of alcohol consumption to mortality and to the risk of cardiovascular events in a large cohort of men followed from age 18 up to 55.
the relationship between alcohol consumption and mortality and cardiovascular events, and the role of alcohol as an independent risk factor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
alcohol consumption in moderation is associated with a reduced risk for all-cause, cardiovascular and coronary heart disease mortality.
moderate alcohol consumption is associated with a lower risk of mortality and cardiovascular events.
alcohol consumption is a risk factor for all-cause mortality in men and in women.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found no evidence that alcohol consumption was associated with mortality and cardiovascular events among men and women up to age 50-55.
the association of heavy alcohol use and mortality and cardiovascular events is U shaped.
alcohol consumption in moderation is associated with reduced risk of cardiovascular events, but that heavy drinking increases the risk of mortality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relationship between alcohol and cardiovascular disease is not as straightforward as previously thought.
alcohol consumption has a J-shaped relationship with mortality and cardiovascular events.
alcohol consumption is not a risk factor for cardiovascular disease in men, and it may be protective in women.
